## Two things land on your desk the same week

Release B — VAL-1203's upgrade, the BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) upgrade this
course has followed for five modules — has been live in production for a full quarter now. No
open deviations, training done, the version mismatch module 2 caught long since reconciled.

Two things arrive almost together.

First: the vendor's first quarterly OS (operating system) security patch for the new release. A
medium-severity CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — the industry's standard identifier
for a publicly disclosed security flaw), vendor advisory attached, release notes describing it as
touching "OS-level memory handling only." If that sentence sounds familiar, it should. It's almost
exactly what opened this course.

Second: BECS's first periodic review since the upgrade is due. Nobody invented this requirement
out of nowhere — it's on Lakeshore's own validation calendar, the way any validated system's
ongoing-fitness check would be. Its scope line reads: "cumulative change history since BECS was
last proven to work end to end." That history is longer than one quarter. It reaches back through
VAL-1203's own cutover, through the Friday OS patch that became VIA-0842 — the open question this
course was built to answer, closed as history two courses ago — through DEV-1147 (the ICCBBA
product-code-table push that left roughly forty units one revision behind on label text, caught
before anything shipped), and through a separate, earlier off-hours BECS configuration change
whose post-deployment check failed on the label-printer interface.

Your Quality Validation Lead is handling the new patch exactly the way this module is about to
describe. Your periodic review, meanwhile, is about to do something this course has postponed
twice already: look straight at VIA-0842 and say, finally, whether twelve tests were enough. No
citations yet. No verdict yet. Both are coming.

## Why this rule exists, and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure this module exists to prevent: a system gets validated once, carefully, and
then slowly stops being the system that was proven to work — not through one dramatic change, but
through a string of small ones, each defensible on its own, none of them re-examined together. A
validated state isn't a status you earn and keep. It's a claim that has to survive every single
thing that happens to the system afterward, for as long as the system runs.

You already own the ITSM (IT service management) vocabulary for most of this. **Patch
management** and **release and deployment management** are practices you run routinely: patches
arrive on a cadence, get tested, get scheduled, get deployed. A **CAB (change advisory board)**
gives a change its final look before it ships. And you already know the concept of a **standard
change** — a change type so well understood, so low-risk, and so consistently executed the same
way that it's pre-approved by class, instead of re-litigated from scratch every time one comes up.

Here's where the regulated world asks for something your CAB's "standard change" category doesn't,
by itself, supply. A standard change is pre-approved because its *risk* is well understood. For
BECS, "well understood" has to mean something specific: somebody has actually analyzed what a patch
of this *kind* does to the whole system, not just confirmed it installs cleanly on a test server.
That distinction — install evidence versus analysis evidence — is this module's spine, and it's
exactly where VIA-0842 went wrong.

There's a real tension underneath all of this, worth naming honestly instead of picking a side. A
security team wants patches applied fast — an unpatched medium-severity CVE is its own live risk,
sitting on a production server, every day it waits. A validated system can't just absorb an
unvalidated change without undermining the entire reason "validated" means anything. Treating those
two pressures as a forced choice — patch immediately and skip validation, or stay vulnerable for
months waiting on a full revalidation cycle — is a false choice. The real fix, and this module's
main practical idea, is a fast path that's still validated: regression analysis and regression
testing, pre-scoped once per patch *class*, so a well-understood patch doesn't reinvent its test
plan from nothing every time one ships.

One more risk decision, named here and not developed further: running a release past its vendor's
end-of-support date, or deciding exactly when to force an upgrade instead, is itself an owned risk
decision — the same kind this curriculum's quality-risk-management module already taught you to
demand be written down and signed, not defaulted into by inaction. VAL-1203 exists because
Lakeshore made that call once already. It won't be the last time.

## The rule in plain English

**First: a vendor's characterization of a patch is an input, never an analysis.** "OS-level memory
handling only" is a real, useful fact — it tells you something about what the vendor believes it
changed. It is not evidence about what that change actually touches once it's running inside
*your* system, against *your* configuration, under *your* load. The regulatory floor behind
Lakeshore's own validation obligation, 21 CFR 211.68(a), already quoted in full back in module 1,
requires a written program that keeps the system performing the way it's designed to, on a routine
basis — and FDA's BECS guidance (guidance tier, not binding regulation) is explicit that for a
*change*, what makes that program adequate is Lakeshore's own documented regression analysis, not a
characterization borrowed from someone else's release notes.

**Second: regression analysis and regression testing are two different steps, in order.**
Regression *analysis* comes first: a documented look at what the change could plausibly affect
across the whole system, not just the piece it was aimed at. Regression *testing* comes second,
and its scope is supposed to follow from what the analysis found — not from a number that felt
defensible, and not from a vendor's say-so. An OS patch that touches memory handling plausibly
affects anything with timing or concurrency sensitivity: label-print jobs, instrument interfaces,
anything running under real load. A regression analysis is the document that's supposed to say so
in writing, before a test plan gets written, not after.

**Third: not every patch needs that analysis written from scratch.** This is where a mature
validation program earns its keep, and it's industry practice, not anything a regulation names.
Classify patch *types* once — an "OS security patch, no application code change" is one class; a
"vendor hotfix to a named BECS module" is a different class; an "infrastructure or network
change" is a third — and pre-analyze, for each class, what kind of regression testing it plausibly
requires. The next time a patch in that class arrives, its validation impact assessment (VIA,
module 1's and VIA-0842's own term) starts from that template instead of reasoning out the
regression question from zero. This is the direct cousin of your CAB's standard-change category,
one layer deeper: the category still gets a per-instance VIA, with Quality's blocking sign-off,
same as `becs-in-the-pipeline` established from the start — but that VIA now starts pre-scoped
correctly, instead of resting on whatever the vendor's advisory happened to say.

This quarter's patch is the positive version of that story. Your Validation Lead classified it
immediately: OS security patch, no application code change — the same class VIA-0842 was. Instead
of asking "does the vendor say this is safe," the VIA opened with a regression analysis: what does
an OS-level memory-handling change plausibly touch across BECS as a whole? The answer pulled in
label-print timing, the instrument interfaces, and the testing-lab result feed — not because
anyone suspected a specific defect, but because that's what the analysis, not the vendor, said to
look at. The test plan that followed was scoped to that analysis. That's the whole difference this
module is built to teach, and you're watching it work in real time, on the same kind of patch that
went wrong once already.

### Periodic review: checking whether "validated" is still true

Patching is one way a validated state can drift. **Periodic review** is the practice that's
supposed to catch drift from *everything*, on a schedule, whether or not any single change looked
risky enough to trigger a second look on its own. It's industry practice — GAMP's own concept,
named and described here in the course's own words, never quoted; GAMP is copyrighted and this
course doesn't cite it like a regulation — not a regulatory requirement with its own numbered
clause. Its regulatory hooks are real, just looser than a checklist: 211.68(a)'s "routinely...
checked according to a written program," already quoted above, and the guidance's own phrase for
cadence, quoted in full below — "on a routine basis." Neither sentence says how often. That's
Lakeshore's own call, made and documented, not handed down.

A periodic review that's actually doing its job looks at several things together, not one at a
time:

- **The cumulative change history** since the system was last proven end to end — VAL-1203's own
  cutover, the OS patch that became VIA-0842, DEV-1147's table push, and the earlier off-hours
  configuration change that failed its label-printer check. Looked at individually, each got its
  own disposition at the time. Looked at together, a pattern can show up that no single review
  would have caught.
- **Deviations, incidents, and problem records** — not re-litigated, just surveyed for anything
  pointing at the same underlying weakness more than once.
- **The vendor's own unresolved-anomalies list** — module 4's subject, named here only as something
  a thorough review would pull back out and re-check against what's happened since.
- **Configuration drift against the validated baseline.** The one check a non-technical reviewer
  wouldn't think to make, and it's yours specifically: does what's actually running still match
  what was last validated, or has it drifted through small, individually-approved changes nobody
  looked at in aggregate? Same instinct that caught VAL-1203's database-version mismatch in module
  2 — the guidance's own instruction to validate a configuration and move that *same* configuration
  into production (III.G) — run now across a whole quarter instead of one cutover weekend.
- **Access reviews** — module 5's closed-system territory, not re-taught here, just checked: does
  who can touch BECS still match who's supposed to be able to.

A periodic review can conclude three different things: the validated state is confirmed, as is;
targeted revalidation is needed on a specific function or interface; or a finding is serious enough
to open a CAPA (corrective and preventive action). This quarter's review is about to produce the
third outcome — but not against the patch that just shipped correctly. Against a patch that
shipped a quarter *before* this upgrade ever started.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 211.68(a) | "Two-eleven point sixty-eight, paragraph a" | A written program must keep automated equipment, including computers, performing satisfactorily, with routine checks and records. | The floor every patch's VIA and every periodic review exists to satisfy — quoted in full back in module 1. |
| Guidance III.C | "Section three, part C" | A written plan isn't "designed to assure proper performance" unless it requires validation prior to routine use, on a routine basis, and any time a change is made that could affect the system's functions. | The cadence hook behind periodic review, and the sequencing problem in VIA-0842's own record. |
| Guidance III.G (post-implementation monitoring) | "Section three, part G" | Recommends closely monitoring the system for a period after installing new or upgraded software, to catch anything the test cases missed. | What VIA-0842's record never shows happened after its 10:15 p.m. deployment. |
| Guidance III.I | "Section three, part I" | A software regression analysis of the change's impact on the *entire* system should be conducted for any change, however small; regression testing should follow from that analysis, including by re-running previously passed cases. | The adequacy check's Regression question — and the exact requirement VIA-0842's twelve tests were never shown to satisfy. |

## The actual text

Validation after a change, quoted in full from
`sources/fda-guidance/becs-validation-users-facility-2013.md`, section III.I — the text this whole
module, and this course's central verdict, rests on:

> When the BECS manufacturer modifies the software, the manufacturer should inform you of other
> functions that might be affected. We recommend that your contract with a software manufacturer
> specifically address this issue. However, you are ultimately responsible for assuring that the
> system used in your establishment has been validated for use in your establishment.

> Due to the complexity of systems and BECS, a seemingly small local change (e.g., software,
> hardware, peripherals, or infrastructure) may have a significant global system effect. When any
> change (even a small change) is made to the software on the system, a software regression
> analysis should be conducted, not just for validation of the individual change, but also to
> determine the extent and impact of that change on the entire system. Based on the analysis, you
> should then conduct an appropriate level of software regression testing to show that unchanged
> but vulnerable portions of the system have not been adversely affected. Appropriate regression
> analysis and testing provide the confidence that the system is validated after a software change
> (Ref. 2). We recommend that you perform regression testing, when indicated by your analysis, by
> re-running test cases that previously passed.

Read that first paragraph carefully: "the manufacturer *should* inform you" and "we recommend that
your contract... address this issue" are both guidance-tier, both squarely about the vendor
relationship — named here, not developed; vendor contract mechanics belong to a future course. The
sentence that actually binds the outcome is the one after it: "you are ultimately responsible." The
vendor's characterization of its own patch was always an input to that responsibility. It was never
a substitute for it.

On cadence, section III.C, already quoted in module 1 for a different point, requoted here for this
module's own:

> A written plan is not "designed to assure proper performance" unless it requires user validation
> prior to routine use, on a routine basis, and any time a change is made that has the potential to
> affect the functions of the system.

"On a routine basis" is the guidance's own cadence phrase — and notice it never says how routine.
No number of months or years is in that sentence anywhere.

On watching a system after it goes live, from section III.G:

> We recommend that you closely monitor the system for a period of time after installation of the
> new or upgraded software in the production environment to detect any discrepancies that were not
> identified by the test cases.

That sentence is this module's answer to "what happens after the twelve tests pass." Testing,
however well scoped, can't catch everything. A monitoring period afterward is the guidance's own
backstop for whatever testing missed — and it's a step VIA-0842's own record never shows anyone
took.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) assessor
reviewing a patch VIA wouldn't ask whether it installed cleanly. They'd ask for the document that
shows Lakeshore reasoned about the *whole system*, not just the patch's stated target: **a dated
regression analysis, written before the test plan**, naming what it considered and ruled in or out
— not a sentence that restates the vendor's advisory. They'd also ask whether a failed test during
execution got treated as new information or noise: a test that fails once, gets re-run to a pass,
and is closed with no discrepancy note is the fastest way an inspector's confidence in the rest of
the package collapses, because it suggests the team was managing to a result, not reading one. And
they'd check whether the periodic review actually reaches back across the full change history, not
one that resets its clock at the last upgrade — "we reviewed this quarter" is a weaker answer than
"we reviewed everything that's happened to this system, including the patch two releases ago that
never got a regression analysis."

A bad answer to "why wasn't this patch's regression scope broader" sounds like "the vendor told us
it was OS-level only." A good answer points to a dated analysis that reasoned past the vendor's own
words.

## Common traps

**"Our last periodic review set an annual cadence, so that's now Lakeshore's regulatory
deadline."** No regulation sets any fixed revalidation frequency. 211.68(a) requires routine checks
"according to a written program," and the guidance's own phrase is "on a routine basis" (III.C) —
neither names a number. An annual cadence can be exactly the right, risk-based choice, and once
Lakeshore writes it down it should keep it — but it's Lakeshore's own industry-practice decision
(GAMP's periodic-review concept), not a clause anyone could cite back as the law.

**"The patch installed without errors, so it's validated."** The trap VIA-0842 fell into, dressed
differently. A clean install is implementation evidence — proof the patch deployed as intended. It
says nothing about whether the unchanged, potentially vulnerable, parts of the system still work.
Only a regression analysis, followed by regression testing scoped to that analysis, can show that.

## What this means for your job

- **Before co-signing any patch VIA, ask for the regression analysis, not the vendor's advisory.**
  If the whole argument for a reduced test scope is a sentence from the vendor's release notes,
  send it back — that's an input, never the analysis itself.
- **Build and maintain patch-class templates with your Validation Lead**, so a well-understood
  patch type starts its VIA pre-scoped instead of reinventing the question every quarter. This is
  the single highest-leverage systemic fix you can push for after this module.
- **Treat a test that fails once and passes on re-run as a signal about scope, not a nuisance to
  clear.** If nobody wrote down why it failed the first time, ask before you sign — especially on
  anything timing- or load-sensitive.
- **Read a periodic review for whether it reaches back across the system's whole history**, not
  just since the last big project closed — a review scoped to "this quarter" will miss exactly the
  kind of drift this module is built to catch.
- **Treat configuration-drift checks as your own job, every cycle.** Nobody else on the review is
  positioned to pull the CMDB (configuration management database) and ask whether what's running
  still matches what was last validated. That's the Director-only catch, every time.

## VIA-0842, finally: were twelve tests enough

This course opened by naming VIA-0842 as the reason it exists. Here's the answer, and it's not the
one either side of that original debate was arguing for.

**The number twelve was never actually the question.** It sounds like it should have been — more
tests feels safer than fewer — but chasing the right number was always a distraction from the real
defect. VIA-0842's twelve test cases were never derived from a documented regression analysis of
the patch's impact on the whole system. They rested entirely on the vendor's own characterization:
"OS-level memory handling only." That sentence is a vendor **input**. It was never Lakeshore's own
**analysis**. An OS patch that touches memory handling plausibly affects anything with timing or
concurrency sensitivity — which, on a BECS server, means instrument interfaces, the hospital
interface, and label-print timing under real, peak-load conditions, not just the normal-volume
check the primary print station actually got. None of those three made it into the twelve-test
scope. A real regression analysis would have had reason to pull in exactly those three. Nobody
wrote one, so nobody found that reason, so none of them made it into the test plan.

**Step 7's own first-run failure was itself the evidence that got ignored.** Step 7 — label-print
job timing, at the primary print station — failed on its first run, was re-run the same day, passed
on re-run, and closed with no discrepancy note. That's not a footnote. A timing-sensitive test
failing once, right after a memory-handling patch, is the system telling you something directly
relevant to scope. The correct response to that signal was to widen the test scope — ask what else
timing-sensitive might be affected — not to re-run the same case until it went green and move on as
if nothing had happened.

**Here's the two-layer lesson, in one real document.** `directing-the-quality-analyst` already
reviewed VIA-0842 once, using the cold-read test: would this document survive an inspector reading
it cold, with its author not in the room? That review found the twelve-test scope was a
deliberately planted *non-gap* at that layer — the Director couldn't judge whether twelve tests
were sufficient, but the rationale for the scope was documented and signed, "Scope and rationale
reviewed: Quality Validation Lead, 11/06." At the decision-trail layer, VIA-0842 held up. That
finding doesn't change today, and this module doesn't reopen it.

But this course built a second instrument specifically because the first one can't answer every
question: the adequacy check, and its fourth question, **Regression** — named since module 2,
applied for the first time right here. Does a documented analysis of the change's impact on the
*whole* system exist, and does the testing that followed actually follow from that analysis, not
just from a vendor's say-so? Run VIA-0842 through that question, and the answer is no. No
regression analysis exists anywhere in its record. The scope rested on the vendor's words, not
Lakeshore's reasoning. **A package can pass layer 1 and fail layer 2, in the same document, at the
same time.** VIA-0842 is exactly that case — and it's the reason "defensible" has needed two
different meanings since this course's first page.

There's a third thread, easy to miss next to the first two, and it's more than a paperwork problem.
VIA-0842's protocol — its fixed acceptance criteria — wasn't approved until Wednesday 11/11. Its
twelve tests had already executed Monday through Tuesday, 11/09–11/10, *before* that approval
existed. Production deployment followed that same Wednesday, 10:15 p.m. Read that sequence against
section III.C, quoted above: a written plan isn't "designed to assure proper performance" unless it
requires validation "prior to routine use... and any time a change is made." You cannot prove a
test was judged against criteria that didn't yet exist when the test ran. That's not a dating
technicality. It undermines the entire premise of having fixed acceptance criteria at all.

**None of this reopens VIA-0842.** `directing-the-quality-analyst`'s later management-review packet
already reported it, accurately, as closed — "closed this cycle, with a decision-trail gap
corrected before production sign-off." That stays true. Nothing above is a new reportable
deviation, and nothing above rewrites a single fact in VIA-0842's own record. What's different is
that this periodic review, looking back at closed history with a second instrument the curriculum
didn't have until now, draws a finding the first review had no way to reach: the testing was never
shown to be adequate, because no regression analysis ever justified its own scope.

**Right-sized remediation follows directly from that finding, and proportion matters here as much
as the finding itself.** Two things, not one sweeping one: a documented regression analysis for the
OS-patch class, going forward, so the next patch like this one starts correctly scoped — exactly
what your Validation Lead already did for this quarter's patch, which is why it's the positive
contrast sitting right next to this finding. And targeted supplemental testing now, against the
*currently running system*, aimed at the three places VIA-0842's analysis should have reached:
instrument interfaces, the hospital interface, and label-print timing under peak load. That's not a
reflexive full revalidation of everything BECS does — the finding doesn't call for that, and asking
for it would be its own kind of overcorrection. It's also not a retroactive rewrite of VIA-0842's
record. It's confirming, now, that the functions nobody tested back then actually are fine, which is
exactly what VIA-0842's own open item — "BECS-to-hospital interface regression testing to follow,"
never assigned an owner or a date — was always going to require eventually anyway.

If this periodic review wants a formal quality-system outcome, the proportionate one is a CAPA, not
on VIA-0842 itself, but on the VIA template and procedure: require a documented regression analysis
before any VIA can approve a reduced test scope, for every future patch, every class, every time.
That's the systemic version of the fix your Validation Lead already applied, once, to this
quarter's patch. A periodic-review finding that produces that fix is the methodological payoff of
everything this course has built. A periodic-review finding that tries to retroactively discipline
a closed deviation is not the same thing, and isn't what this finding calls for.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: "Validated systems must be fully revalidated every year." Accurate?

No. No regulation sets a fixed revalidation frequency — annual or otherwise. 21 CFR 211.68(a)
requires routine checks "according to a written program," and FDA's guidance says validation should
happen "on a routine basis" (III.C), but neither sentence names a number. The actual cadence is
Lakeshore's own risk-based choice, using periodic review as industry practice (GAMP's own concept)
— not a regulatory mandate of once a year or any other fixed interval. Once Lakeshore writes a
cadence down and commits to it, that commitment matters. It just isn't a rule anyone could cite back
as "the law requires annual revalidation," because no rule says that.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: This quarter's OS patch installed cleanly in staging, with no errors. Does that mean it's validated?

No, and this is exactly the trap VIA-0842 fell into once already. A clean install is implementation
evidence — proof the patch deployed the way it was supposed to. The regulated question is a
different one entirely: do the unchanged, but potentially vulnerable, parts of the system still
work the way they did before the patch. Only a documented regression analysis, followed by
regression testing scoped to what that analysis found, can answer that (guidance III.I). "It
deployed without errors" and "it's validated" are two separate facts, and only a regression
analysis connects them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Someone on the quality team says, "`directing-the-quality-analyst` already reviewed VIA-0842's decision trail and found it held up — so the testing question is already settled." Right?

Only half right, and the half that's wrong is the important half. `directing-the-quality-analyst`'s
cold-read review found VIA-0842's decision trail held up: the twelve-test scope was documented and
signed, "Scope and rationale reviewed: Quality Validation Lead, 11/06." That finding is real and
this module doesn't change it. But that review was explicitly checking whether the *story* held
together, not whether the *testing* was technically adequate — it told the Director, at the time, to
route that second question elsewhere, because the method to answer it didn't exist yet. This
course's adequacy check, specifically its Regression question, is that method, and applying it to
VIA-0842 finds something the first review had no way to find: no documented regression analysis
ever justified the twelve-test scope. Both findings are true at once, about the same document. A
package can pass the decision-trail layer and fail the technical-adequacy layer at the same time.
:::

## Where this goes next

You can now run a change through regression analysis instead of a vendor's characterization, build
patch-class templates that start a VIA correctly scoped, design a periodic review that catches
drift nobody else would think to check for, and give VIA-0842's twelve tests a real, methodological
verdict instead of a number anyone could argue with. What's still sitting open is VIA-0842's own
unfinished business: "BECS-to-hospital interface regression testing to follow," never assigned an
owner, and the instrument-interface test its twelve-test scope never included in the first place.
That's `becs-interfaces-and-data-integrity`, next — where every boundary BECS touches, instruments
in, labels out, hospitals downstream, finally gets the interface-specific validation this module
pointed toward but didn't build.
